title: Loops
description: for, enhanced for, while, and do-while loops, plus break, continue, and nested loops.
objectives: Write classic and enhanced for loops
Use break and continue, including in nested loops
Choose the right loop type for a given task

content.heading: for, Enhanced for, while, and do-while
content.body:
The classic for loop, for (init; condition; update) { ... }, is ideal when you need explicit control over an index or counter. The enhanced for loop (also called for-each), for (Type item : collection) { ... }, iterates directly over the elements of an array or any Iterable (like an ArrayList), without manual index management — preferred whenever you don't actually need the index itself.

while (condition) { ... } checks its condition before each iteration, suited to loops with an unknown number of iterations. do { ... } while (condition); checks its condition after each iteration, guaranteeing the body runs at least once even if the condition starts false — useful for input-validation loops that must prompt at least one time.

content.heading: break, continue, and Nested Loops
content.body: break immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop (or switch); continue skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds to the loop's next check/update. In nested loops, both break and continue by default only affect the innermost loop they're written in — Java supports labeled break/continue (outer: for (...) { for (...) { break outer; } }) to affect a specifically named outer loop, an escape hatch used sparingly, since restructuring the logic (e.g., with a flag variable or extracting a method with early return) is usually clearer.

content.explanation: The enhanced for reads each array element without index bookkeeping. continue outer skips straight to the outer loop's next iteration, bypassing the rest of the inner loop entirely — a labeled loop control statement.

keyPoints: Classic for gives explicit index control; enhanced for iterates elements directly
do-while guarantees at least one execution of the loop body
break/continue affect only the nearest enclosing loop by default
Labeled break/continue (label: ... break label;) can target a specific outer loop
commonMistakes: Using an enhanced for loop when the index itself is actually needed
Forgetting a do-while's semicolon after the while(condition)
Using unlabeled break/continue inside nested loops and being surprised it only affects the inner loop
